ai.definition: Digital Physics Simulation is a computational framework that models and simulates physical phenomena using digital means. It allows researchers to create virtual universes where they can test hypotheses, develop technologies, and explore complex systems without the need for physical prototypes or experiments.
ai.howItWorks: By leveraging advanced algorithms and high-performance computing, Digital Physics Simulation creates detailed simulations of physical laws and processes. These simulations can range from quantum mechanics at microscopic scales to cosmology at macroscopic scales, providing a platform for testing theories and developing technologies in a controlled digital environment.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the challenges of prototyping and experimenting with complex systems that are difficult or impossible to study using traditional methods due to cost, time constraints, or safety concerns. This technology enables rapid iteration and exploration of theoretical concepts before physical implementation.
ai.manufacturing: Not directly related as it is a simulation tool rather than a manufacturing process itself. However, it can significantly reduce the need for physical prototypes by providing detailed simulations that guide design and development processes.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves developing algorithms to accurately model physical phenomena, integrating these models into a computational framework, and optimizing performance through high-performance computing techniques such as parallel processing and GPU acceleration.
ai.costDrivers: High-performance computing resources, advanced algorithm development, and the complexity of modeling real-world systems. The cost can be significant due to the need for powerful hardware and skilled personnel.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: growing adoption in research and development sectors, with potential for broader applications as computational power increases and algorithms become more sophisticated.
ai.regulation: Currently not heavily regulated but may face regulatory scrutiny if used in contexts where it could impact public safety or intellectual property rights. Regulations will likely evolve as the technology matures and its applications expand.
ai.risks: Risk of inaccurate modeling leading to misinformed decisions, potential for computational errors, and ethical concerns related to virtual experimentation on complex systems.
ai.profitability: Potential for high profitability in sectors like pharmaceuticals, materials science, and advanced manufacturing where it can significantly reduce development costs. However, the initial investment is substantial.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include more accurate models of physical phenomena, integration with machine learning techniques to improve predictive capabilities, and increased accessibility through cloud computing services.

glossary.def: A computational framework that models and simulates physical phenomena using digital means.
Advanced computing resources designed to handle complex simulations and data processing tasks efficiently.
The branch of physics dealing with the behavior of matter and energy on a microscopic scale, particularly subatomic particles.
The study of the large-scale structure, origin, and evolution of the universe.

subsystems.name: Discretisation layer
subsystems.role: represents space, time and quantum fields on a finite lattice.

subsystems.name: State store
subsystems.role: holds the amplitudes of the quantum state being evolved.

subsystems.name: Processor fabric
subsystems.role: applies the time-evolution operators to the stored state.

subsystems.name: Energy and heat rejection
subsystems.role: supplies power and dumps waste heat, which sets the cost of every irreversible operation.

subsystems.name: Algorithms and validation
subsystems.role: turns the state into measurable predictions and checks them against known physics.

buildSteps.title: Choose a discretisation
buildSteps.detail: Space–time is chopped into a grid with a minimum spacing. Unknown Planck-scale physics means the choice is a guess; the simulation is only as good as the theory fed into it.

buildSteps.title: Bound the information content
buildSteps.detail: Use the Bekenstein bound — maximum information in a region scales with its surface area and energy — to estimate the bits needed. A Planck-scale description of the observable universe implies on the order of 10^180–10^185 cells, far more than any ordinary computer can hold.

buildSteps.title: Bound the operations and energy
buildSteps.detail: The Margolus–Levitin limit caps operations per second at roughly 2E/πħ for energy E, and Landauer's principle sets a floor of kT ln2 per irreversible bit. Multiplying these out shows the energy required dwarfs the mass-energy of the observable universe, so the scheme fails long before hardware is considered.

buildSteps.title: Pick a substrate
buildSteps.detail: A classical machine must carry all amplitudes explicitly — exponentially expensive. A quantum simulator instead maps the simulated system onto controllable quantum degrees of freedom, which is why quantum simulation, not brute-force digital emulation, is the only credible route.

buildSteps.title: Build the hardware
buildSteps.detail: Assemble error-corrected quantum processors with many physical qubits per logical qubit, plus the classical control electronics and cryogenics they need.

buildSteps.title: Scale up power and cooling
buildSteps.detail: Any star-scale version — sometimes imagined as a Matrioshka brain, nested shells of computing around a star — would need enormous collectors and radiators, and would run near the 2.7 K cosmic background temperature to keep erasure costs low.

buildSteps.title: Write and compile the simulation
buildSteps.detail: Encode the field theory onto the hardware, compile the time-evolution circuit and run repeated shots to build statistics.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against reality
buildSteps.detail: Validate against measured particle masses, cross-sections and cosmological observations; if the model misses them, the discretisation or physics is wrong.

buildSteps.title: Run and query
buildSteps.detail: Extract observables, compare alternative discretisations, and treat disagreement as the error bar on any conclusion.

prerequisites.why: quantum simulation is exponentially cheaper than classical, but error-corrected machines of the needed size do not exist.
theoretical mappings from physical systems to controllable quantum hardware were worked out from the 1980s onward; the missing part is hardware, not theory.
without it, there is no justified rule for what happens at or below the Planck scale, so a Planck-scale simulation has no correct physics to implement.
Landauer's principle, the Margolus–Levitin limit and the Bekenstein bound let us estimate feasibility — and currently show it fails by an astronomical margin.
the energy and heat-rejection infrastructure implied by a Matrioshka-brain concept is speculative and beyond any known manufacturing path.

pathway.milestone: classical simulation of lattice field theories and small quantum systems on supercomputers
pathway.unlocks: predictions for particle and materials physics where exact calculation is impossible.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant quantum computers running quantum simulation of systems no classical machine can handle
pathway.unlocks: chemistry, materials and nuclear physics beyond classical reach.

pathway.milestone: large analog quantum simulators reproducing condensed-matter and cosmological toy models
pathway.unlocks: tests of fundamental physics using controllable quantum systems.

pathway.milestone: star-scale computing, if it is possible at all
pathway.unlocks: nothing that current energy accounting supports: the estimated Landauer cost of a Planck-scale universe simulation exceeds the energy content of the observable universe, so this remains a thought experiment rather than an engineering programme.
